title: MYP Language Acquisition Criteria A-D Explained
summary: MYP Language Acquisition criteria explained clearly: understand Criteria A-D, decode teacher feedback, and learn what a high-band response requires.
body_markdown:
A student opens a marked language assessment and sees four separate scores. Criterion A: 6. Criterion B: 7. Criterion C: 5. Criterion D: 6.


The numbers look precise, but they do not immediately explain what to do next. That is the real challenge of the **MYP Language Acquisition criteria** . A grade records where your performance landed; useful feedback reveals how to move it.


The current framework separates language performance into four areas: listening, reading, speaking and writing. Each criterion has a maximum achievement level of 8. However, the exact descriptor depends on whether the course is at the emergent, capable or proficient level, so students should always use the task-specific rubric supplied by their teacher.


This guide follows a hypothetical student reading teacher feedback and translating it into practical action.


### MYP Language Acquisition criteria at a glance


Criterion Assessed skill Central question


A Listening Can you understand and interpret spoken multimodal texts?


B Reading Can you understand and interpret written multimodal texts?


C Speaking Can you communicate an appropriate, organized message orally?


D Writing Can you communicate an appropriate, organized message in writing?


The[IB overview of MYP Language Acquisition](https://www.ibo.org/programmes/middle-years-programme/curriculum/language-acquisition/) identifies three broad proficiency levels: emergent, capable and proficient. The complexity of texts and expected language change across those levels, but the four-part structure remains recognizable.


Do not confuse Language Acquisition with[MYP Language and Literature](https://www.ibo.org/programmes/middle-years-programme/curriculum/language-and-literature/) . Language Acquisition concerns learning an additional language, while Language and Literature follows a different curriculum and assessment structure.


A student uses an enormous magnifying glass to search for the secret to full marks while a teacher suggests reading the next sentence of the feedback


### MYP Language Acquisition criterion A: Listening


Imagine the student's feedback says:


> You understood the main message and most stated details, but your explanation of the speaker's attitude needed stronger evidence.


This means Criterion A is not simply testing whether the student heard the words. It asks whether the student can make meaning from a spoken multimodal text, such as a video, interview or presentation combining speech with visual information.


Depending on the proficiency level, the assessment may ask students to identify explicit information, infer implicit meaning, recognize conventions and explain connections. Explicit information is directly stated. Implicit meaning must be inferred from evidence such as tone, emphasis, context or the relationship between spoken and visual details.


### What a high-band listening response looks like


A high-band response typically:


- identifies relevant facts, opinions, messages and supporting details accurately
- distinguishes what is stated from what is implied
- explains conventions, such as tone, repetition or visual choices
- analyses meaningful connections between ideas or parts of the text
- supports interpretations with precise evidence


The most common mistake is writing a plausible interpretation without showing where it came from. A better answer follows a simple chain: **claim, evidence, explanation** . For example, identify the speaker's attitude, point to the phrase or vocal feature that reveals it, and explain the connection.


Students can use RevisionDojo's **Study Notes** , **Flashcards** and **AI Chat** to review vocabulary and practise explaining meaning instead of merely recalling isolated words.


### Criterion B: Reading


The student turns to the next comment:


> You found the relevant details, but some answers described the image and article separately rather than explaining their connection.


Criterion B assesses comprehension of written multimodal texts. These may combine writing with photographs, layout, typography, charts or other visual and spatial features. Reading the sentences is therefore only part of the task.


A student might correctly state that an advertisement uses a bright image. Analysis begins when the student explains why that image was chosen, how it supports the written message and what response it is intended to create.


### What a high-band reading response looks like


Strong Criterion B work usually:


- retrieves explicit information accurately
- infers unstated ideas from textual and visual evidence
- identifies the text's audience, purpose and message
- analyses conventions rather than merely naming them
- explains connections within the text and, when required, between texts


A useful test is to ask, “Have I explained *how* I know?” If the answer contains only a conclusion, it is probably incomplete. If it connects an interpretation to words, images, structure or context, it is moving toward analysis.


A **Questionbank** can help students practise this repeatedly. RevisionDojo's **Grading tools** can then make the practice more useful by comparing a response with the relevant expectations, rather than treating every correct observation as equally developed.


### Criterion C: Speaking


The third comment reads:


> Your ideas were relevant and generally clear. To move higher, sustain your message, use a wider range of language and make your delivery more purposeful.


Criterion C assesses spoken communication. It is not a test of whether a student has a native-like accent. The central issue is whether the student can communicate a clear, relevant and appropriately organized message for the assigned audience, purpose and context.


The precise requirements vary by proficiency level and task. Teachers may consider vocabulary, grammatical control, pronunciation, intonation, fluency, organization and non-verbal communication. A few minor mistakes do not automatically prevent high achievement if communication remains effective.


### What a high-band speaking response looks like


A strong speaker generally:


- addresses every part of the prompt
- organizes ideas into a coherent progression
- uses varied, task-appropriate vocabulary and structures
- communicates with sustained clarity and fluency
- uses pronunciation and intonation to support meaning
- adapts register and delivery to the audience and purpose


Preparation should focus on structure, not memorizing a script word for word. A memorized answer can become fragile when a question changes. Planning an opening, two or three developed ideas, supporting examples and a conclusion creates flexibility.


Record one attempt, listen back, and revise one weakness at a time. First check whether the message is complete. Then work on organization, language range and delivery. RevisionDojo **Tutors** and **Mock Exams** can add realistic questioning and feedback when independent rehearsal stops revealing new problems.


### Criterion D: Writing


The final comment says:


> The response communicated its purpose, but the register shifted and several ideas needed fuller development.


Criterion D assesses written communication. Good grammar matters, but grammar alone is not the criterion. The writing must also answer the prompt, suit the audience, follow the expected text type and develop a coherent message.


An email to a friend should not sound like a formal public speech. A persuasive article should not become a list of unrelated opinions. Register, format and organization are part of communication because they shape how the reader receives the message.


### What a high-band writing response looks like


High-band writing commonly demonstrates:


- a complete response to the purpose and prompt
- clear organization and developed ideas
- appropriate conventions for the required text type
- suitable register for the audience
- varied vocabulary and sentence structures
- accurate language that keeps communication effective


Before writing, reduce the task to four questions: Who am I? Who is the audience? Why am I writing? What format is required? During revision, check content before correcting individual language errors. A flawless paragraph that ignores half the prompt is still incomplete.


RevisionDojo's **Coursework Library** can help students study how effective responses are shaped, while **Predicted Papers** provide timed opportunities to combine interpretation, planning and language control.


### How to use the MYP Language Acquisition rubric


The rubric is best treated as a map, not a verdict. Begin with the teacher's selected descriptor and compare its verbs with the next band. Words such as *identifies* , *interprets* and *analyses* describe different depths of thinking.


Then turn feedback into one observable action:


- “Add detail” becomes “include two supporting details from the text.”
- “Analyse conventions” becomes “name the feature, cite it and explain its effect.”
- “Improve fluency” becomes “record a two-minute response without restarting.”
- “Use appropriate register” becomes “highlight phrases that do not suit the audience.”


The[IB explanation of MYP assessment](https://www.ibo.org/programmes/middle-years-programme/assessment-and-exams/) also shows why learning to apply skills matters. MYP assessment is designed around subject objectives rather than simple content recall.


### Turning four scores into one useful plan


The student's four numbers now tell a story. Reading is currently strongest. Speaking needs the most immediate attention. Listening and writing share a quieter weakness: evidence and development.


That pattern matters more than chasing four scores at once. Choose one criterion, practise a focused task, compare the response with the rubric and apply the feedback to a second attempt. A rubric becomes useful when its language changes the next piece of work. That is the point of the MYP Language Acquisition criteria: not merely to label performance, but to show what better communication looks like.
